title: Tend and keep
hookLine: the first human is put in the garden to dress it and keep it (Genesis 2:15)
carry: ours to grow, and ours to guard

lines: TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.
cards: Before the serpent, before the fruit, before anyone hides among the trees, there's already a job. Genesis tells it this way: “And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.”
Not to sit on a throne. Not to rest forever in the shade. To dress it, and to keep it.
In this story, work arrives before anything goes wrong. Today: shamar.

teach.b: First, the order. Earlier in the same chapter, before the man is formed, the earth waits, because, the text says, “there was not a man to till the ground.” The garden needs a gardener.
So when work gets talked about as a punishment, Genesis two answers quietly: the work came first. The hard part comes tomorrow, in chapter three.
Second, dress it. In older English, to dress a garden is to work it: to dig and prune and water and weed. It's the hands-in-the-dirt verb, the one that makes things grow.

teach.h: KEEP IT: GUARD AND WATCH OVER.
teach.b: To keep, here, is to guard and watch over. In the King James text the same verb turns up in the priestly blessing: “The LORD bless thee, and keep thee.”

Some readers note that the Hebrew behind both is the same guarding word, shamar. So the keeping asked of the gardener echoes the keeping the blessing asks of God. The gardener isn't only a laborer, but a guardian.
Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary workday.
Put the two verbs side by side and they make a picture of care.
In this story the garden isn't the gardener's to use up. It's the gardener's to make grow and to protect.
Some Jewish and Christian readers have drawn from this verse a way of thinking about the earth, and about anything put into human hands: a job, a child, a row of tomatoes, a team that depends on you.
Some of it is ours to grow, some ours to guard, and often the same thing asks for both.

how: Some Jewish and Christian readers point to Genesis 2:15 when they speak of work as care, and some communities read it as a call to look after the earth.

o: to guard and watch over, as a keeper does
to rule over the land as its owner
to plow and plant a field each spring

games.q: the garden's job — tap the pairs.
p: dig, prune, water: make it grow

s: in Genesis, work only begins as a punishment after the fruit
in chapter two the man is put in the garden to dress it and keep it, before anything goes wrong.
in the King James text, the priestly blessing uses the same word, keep
“The LORD bless thee, and keep thee” (Numbers 6:24).
the garden in Genesis 2 is the man's to use up
the job is to dress it and to keep it: to grow and to guard.

games.q: you're the first gardener, and the garden is in your hands. in the text, what's the job?
o: rule it and use it up.
games.why: Genesis 2:15: to dress it and to keep it. work comes before the fall, as care.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing in your care, a plant, a pet, a bike, a friendship gone quiet, and look at it the way a gardener looks at a row.
Ask what it needs to grow or work well, water, a repair, a call, and that's the dressing; then ask what it needs protecting from, neglect, rushing, a careless hand, and that's the keeping.
If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Shamar. The Hebrew word behind 'keep' in the garden and in the priestly blessing: to guard and watch over. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: to keep, guard, watch over; the keeping in Genesis 2:15.
